unit_label: BRBL Module B unit 1: the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (courseware unit 8)

facts.statement: Purpose and amendments (courseware): the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 was enacted to prevent money laundering and to provide for confiscation of property derived from, or involved in, money laundering. The banking machinery has been used by persons indulging in money laundering, so a separate Chapter, Chapter IV on Obligations of Banking Companies, Financial Institutions and Intermediaries, has been included. The Central Government, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, framed the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records of the Nature and Value of Transactions, etc.) Rules, 2004. The Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Act, 2012 enlarged the definition of money laundering by including activities such as concealment, acquisition, possession and use of proceeds of crime as criminal activities; the 2012 amendment took effect on 15 February 2013. Powers of the Director: Section 13(2) as amended provides that if the Director, in the course of any inquiry, finds that a reporting entity or its designated director on the Board or any of its employees has failed to comply with the obligations under the Chapter, the Director may (a) issue a warning in writing, (b) direct the reporting entity or its designated director or employees to comply with specific instructions, (c) direct them to send reports at such interval as may be prescribed on the measures it is taking, or (d) by an order, levy a fine on the reporting entity or its designated director on the Board or any employees, which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees but may extend to one lakh rupees for each failure. Under the 2012 amendment, Authorised Persons who are Indian Agents under the Money Transfer Service Scheme may nominate a Director on their Boards as Designated Director to ensure compliance. The statute was also amended in 2019.

Offence of money laundering and punishment (courseware): the Act does not define money laundering as such; Section 3 states that whoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime including its concealment, possession, acquisition or use and projecting or claiming it as untainted property shall be guilty of the offence of money laundering. The Explanation clarifies that a person is guilty if found to have directly or indirectly attempted to indulge, assisted knowingly, or been a party to or actually involved in one or more of the processes or activities connected with proceeds of crime: concealment, possession, acquisition, use, projecting as untainted property, or claiming as untainted property in any manner whatsoever; and that the process or activity connected with proceeds of crime is a continuing activity and continues till such time a person is directly or indirectly enjoying the proceeds of crime by its concealment or possession or acquisition or use or projecting it as untainted property or claiming it as untainted property in any manner whatsoever. Punishment (Section 4): whoever commits the offence of money laundering shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine; where the proceeds of crime involved in money laundering relate to any offence specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the words which may extend to seven years are read as which may extend to ten years.

Obligations of reporting entities, Sections 12-15 and enhanced due diligence (courseware): Chapter IV (Sections 12 to 15) sets out obligations. Section 12(1): every reporting entity shall (a) maintain a record of all transactions, including information relating to transactions covered under clause (b), in such manner as to enable it to reconstruct individual transactions; (b) furnish to the Director within such time as may be prescribed information relating to transactions, whether attempted or executed, the nature and value of which may be prescribed; (c) maintain records of documents evidencing identity of its clients and beneficial owners as well as account files and business correspondence relating to its clients. Section 12(2): the information maintained, furnished or verified, save as otherwise provided under any law, shall be kept confidential. Section 12(3): the records referred to in clause (a) are maintained for five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity. Section 12(4): the records referred to in clause (c) are maintained for five years after the business relationship between a client and the reporting entity has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later. Section 12(5): the Central Government may by notification exempt any reporting entity or class of entities from any obligation under the Chapter. The 2019 amendment added Section 12AA on enhanced due diligence: before the commencement of each specified transaction every reporting entity shall verify the identity of the client by authentication under the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016, take additional steps to examine ownership and financial position including sources of funds, and record the purpose behind the specified transaction and the intended nature of the relationship; where the conditions are not fulfilled, the reporting entity shall not allow the specified transaction to be carried out; where any specified transaction or series of transactions undertaken by a client is considered suspicious or likely to involve proceeds of crime, the reporting entity shall increase the future monitoring of the business relationship with the client; the information obtained shall be maintained for five years from the date of transaction. A specified transaction means any withdrawal or deposit in cash exceeding such amount, any transaction in foreign exchange exceeding such amount, any transaction in any high value imports or remittances, and other transactions in the interest of revenue or where there is a high risk of money laundering or terrorist financing. Section 14: no civil or criminal proceedings lie against a reporting entity or its directors or officers for furnishing information to the Director under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 12.

PML Rules: records to be maintained and furnishing of information (courseware): Rule 3 as amended with effect from 27 August 2013 requires every reporting entity to maintain records of: (A) all cash transactions of the value of more than ten lakh rupees or its equivalent in foreign currency; (B) all series of cash transactions integrally connected to each other which have been individually valued below ten lakh rupees or its equivalent in foreign currency where such series of transactions have taken place within a month and the monthly aggregate exceeds ten lakh rupees or its equivalent in foreign currency; (BA) all transactions involving receipts by non-profit organisations of value more than ten lakh rupees or its equivalent in foreign currency; (C) all cash transactions where forged or counterfeit currency notes or bank notes have been used as genuine or where any forgery of a valuable security or a document has taken place facilitating the transaction; (D) all suspicious transactions whether or not made in cash and by way of deposits and credits, withdrawals, money transfer or remittances, loans and advances including credit or loan substitutes, investments and contingent liability (such as commercial paper, certificates of deposit, preferential shares, debentures, securitised participation, inter-bank participation, bills, cheques, foreign exchange contracts, currency, interest rate and commodity derivatives, letters of credit, standby letters of credit, guarantees, comfort letters and solvency certificates), and collection services; (E) all cross border wire transfers of the value of more than five lakh rupees or its equivalent in foreign currency where either the origin or destination of fund is in India; and (F) all purchase and sale by any person of immovable property valued at fifty lakh rupees or more that is registered by the reporting entity. Information in the records (Rule 4): the records shall contain all necessary information specified by the Regulator to permit reconstruction of individual transactions, including the nature of the transactions, the amount of the transaction and the currency in which it was denominated, the date on which the transaction was conducted, and the parties to the transaction. Procedure (Rule 6): the information is maintained in hard and soft copies in accordance with the procedure and manner specified by the Reserve Bank or SEBI. Furnishing information to the Director (Rule 8): the Principal Officer shall furnish the information on transactions in clauses (A), (B), (BA), (C) and (E) every month to the Director by the 15th day of the succeeding month; information on suspicious transactions in clause (D) promptly in writing or by fax or electronic mail not later than seven working days on being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious; information on transactions in clause (F) every quarter to the Director by the 15th day of the month succeeding the quarter. For this rule, delay of each day in not reporting a transaction or delay of each day in rectifying a mis-reported transaction beyond the time limit shall constitute a separate violation.

Verification and maintenance of client identity records (courseware): the Rules prescribe records to be obtained or verified for various types of clients; every banking company shall at the time of opening an account or executing any transaction with it, verify and maintain the record of identity and current address or addresses including permanent address of the client, the nature of business of the client and financial status; if it is not possible to verify the identity at the time of opening or executing the transaction, the banking company verifies the identity within a reasonable time after the account has been opened or the transaction has been executed. Documents: for an individual, one certified copy of an officially valid document containing details of the permanent address, current address and, where applicable, the nature of business and financial status; for a company, the certificate of incorporation, the memorandum and articles of association, a board resolution or power of attorney, and an officially valid document in respect of the person operating the account; for a partnership firm, the registration certificate, the partnership deed and an officially valid document in respect of the person acting in the transaction; for a trust, the registration certificate, the trust deed and an officially valid document in respect of the person acting in the transaction; for an unincorporated association, a resolution of the managing body, a power of attorney granted to the person conducting the transaction and information required to establish the legal existence of the association. Maintenance of identity records: the records relating to the identity of clients shall be maintained for a period of five years from the date of cessation of the transactions between the client and the banking company.

Illustrative cases (courseware): the courseware summarises four cases as illustrations: a Special PMLA court in Kolkata convicted an official of the Rose Valley group, a real estate company that raised money by repeatedly issuing secured non-convertible debentures to many persons; a Special PMLA court in Chennai convicted an importer who made foreign outward remittances through a bank account opened with forged identity documents without disclosing the beneficial owner; a special CBI court convicted a person in a drug related money laundering case in which the Narcotics Control Bureau and the Enforcement Directorate had attached assets; and a Special Court in Ranchi convicted a former State chief minister in 2017, described as the first conviction under the Act of a minister, for laundering funds through companies held in the names of relatives. The courseware states that the Act imposes stringent punishment but that court cases show that penalising under the statute is extremely tedious.

payload.title: Purpose of the Act, the Rules and the Director powers (Section 13)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** the **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002** aims to **prevent money laundering** and to allow **confiscation of property** that comes from it or is used in it. Because **banks have been used by launderers**, **Chapter IV** puts **obligations on banking companies, financial institutions and intermediaries**.

**Rules:** the Central Government framed the **Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records...) Rules, 2004** in consultation with the **Reserve Bank**.

**Amendments:** the **2012 Amendment Act** (effective **15 February 2013**) **widened the definition** of money laundering to include **concealment, acquisition, possession and use** of proceeds of crime; the Act was amended again in **2019**.

**Director's powers (Section 13(2)):** if the **Director** finds a **reporting entity, its designated director or employees** failed to comply, the Director may: (a) give a **written warning**; (b) **direct compliance** with specific instructions; (c) direct **periodic reports** on the measures being taken; or (d) **levy a fine** of **not less than Rs 10,000 and up to Rs 1 lakh for each failure**.

**Money Transfer Service Scheme agents** may nominate a **Designated Director** to ensure compliance.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Act places direct duties on banks and gives the Director graded powers short of prosecution.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the range of the fine the Director may levy for each failure under Section 13(2) as the courseware states?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than Rs 10,000 and up to Rs 1 lakh.

payload.title: The offence of money laundering (Section 3) and punishment (Section 4)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 3:** whoever **directly or indirectly attempts to indulge** or **knowingly assists** or is **knowingly a party** to, or is **actually involved** in, any **process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime**, including its **concealment, possession, acquisition or use**, and **projecting or claiming it as untainted property**, is **guilty of the offence of money laundering**.

**Six activities named:** **concealment**, **possession**, **acquisition**, **use**, **projecting as untainted property** and **claiming as untainted property**.

**A continuing offence:** the process goes on **for as long as the person enjoys the proceeds, directly or indirectly,** in any of these ways.

**Punishment (Section 4):** **rigorous imprisonment of at least three years, up to seven years, and fine**; where the proceeds relate to an offence under **paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule**, the maximum becomes **ten years**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The continuing-offence rule means the offence is not complete when the money is first hidden.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the minimum term of imprisonment for the offence of money laundering under Section 4?

payload.title: Obligations of reporting entities (Sections 12 to 15) and enhanced due diligence (Section 12AA)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 12(1):** every **reporting entity** must: (a) **maintain a record of all transactions** so that **individual transactions can be reconstructed**; (b) **furnish the Director** information on transactions, **attempted or executed**, as prescribed; (c) **maintain identity records** of **clients and beneficial owners**, **account files** and **business correspondence**.

**Section 12(2):** the information is **kept confidential** unless the law provides otherwise.

**Section 12(3):** **transaction records** are kept for **five years from the date of the transaction**.

**Section 12(4):** **identity records** are kept for **five years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later**.

**Section 12(5):** the Central Government may **exempt** a reporting entity or class by notification.

**Enhanced due diligence (Section 12AA, added in 2019):** before each **specified transaction** the entity must **verify the client's identity by Aadhaar authentication**, examine **ownership, financial position and sources of funds**, and **record the purpose and intended nature of the relationship**; if the conditions are **not met**, the transaction **must not be carried out**; suspicious clients are **monitored more closely**; records are kept **five years**. A **specified transaction** includes **cash withdrawals or deposits above a set amount**, **foreign exchange transactions above a set amount**, **high value imports or remittances** and others the Government prescribes.

**Section 14:** a reporting entity, its directors and its officers are protected from **civil and criminal proceedings** for **giving information to the Director**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Safe harbour for reporting encourages banks to report suspicious activity without fear of liability.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long must identity records of clients be kept after the business relationship ends or the account is closed under Section 12(4)?

payload.title: PML Rules: records to be maintained (Rule 3), their contents and procedure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Rule 3 (as amended from 27 August 2013)** requires records of:

| Clause | Transaction |
| --- | --- |
| **(A)** | **All cash transactions of more than Rs 10 lakh** (or equivalent in foreign currency) |
| **(B)** | **Series of connected cash transactions each below Rs 10 lakh** within **a month** whose **monthly total exceeds Rs 10 lakh** |
| **(BA)** | **Receipts by non-profit organisations above Rs 10 lakh** |
| **(C)** | **Cash transactions with forged or counterfeit notes**, or forged securities or documents facilitating the transaction |
| **(D)** | **All suspicious transactions**, cash or otherwise (deposits, withdrawals, transfers, loans, investments, contingent liabilities, guarantees, derivatives and collections) |
| **(E)** | **Cross border wire transfers of more than Rs 5 lakh** where either end is in India |
| **(F)** | **Purchase or sale of immovable property valued at Rs 50 lakh or more** that is **registered by the reporting entity** |

**Contents (Rule 4):** the **nature** of the transaction, the **amount and currency**, the **date**, and the **parties**.

**Form (Rule 6):** kept in **hard and soft copies** as the **Reserve Bank or SEBI** specifies.

**Furnishing to the Director (Rule 8):** the **Principal Officer** sends information on **(A), (B), (BA), (C) and (E)** **monthly by the 15th of the next month**; **suspicious transactions (D)** **promptly, within seven working days** of being satisfied that the transaction is suspicious; **(F)** **quarterly by the 15th of the month after the quarter**. **Each day of delay** or of delay in rectifying a mis-reported transaction is **a separate violation**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The thresholds and deadlines are the working reporting calendar of a bank compliance team.

self_check.prompt_text: By which day of the succeeding month must a Principal Officer report monthly cash transactions to the Director under Rule 8?

payload.title: Verification of the identity of clients and records of identity
payload.core_explanation_md:
**At account opening or transaction:** the bank must **verify and keep** the **identity**, **current and permanent address**, **nature of business** and **financial status** of the client. If it cannot do so at once it verifies **within a reasonable time** after the account is opened or the transaction is executed.

| Client | Documents |
| --- | --- |
| **Individual** | A **certified copy of an officially valid document** showing **permanent address**, current address and, where relevant, **nature of business and financial status** |
| **Company** | **Certificate of incorporation**, **memorandum and articles**, **board resolution or power of attorney**, and an **officially valid document of the person operating the account** |
| **Partnership firm** | **Registration certificate**, **partnership deed**, and an **officially valid document of the person acting** |
| **Trust** | **Registration certificate**, **trust deed**, and an **officially valid document of the person acting** |
| **Unincorporated association** | **Managing body resolution**, **power of attorney** and **information on the association's legal existence** |

**Retention:** records on client identity are kept **five years from the date the transactions with the client cease**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Different entities prove their existence and authority with different papers, but all rely on an officially valid document for the person acting.

self_check.prompt_text: Which document is required for a partnership firm in addition to the registration certificate and the officially valid document of the person acting?

payload.title: Illustrative cases under the Act
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists four convictions to show that the Act is applied to **chit-fund and securities companies**, **false-identity remittances through bank accounts**, **drug related money** and **corruption by a public servant**. It also notes that the Act imposes **stringent punishment**, but that **penalising is tedious** in practice (long trials and complex proceedings).

The individual sentences and fines in the courseware are **not taught** here as they are news-based illustrations.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Cases show how laundering fits the statutory pattern of concealment, possession, acquisition, use and projecting as untainted.

self_check.prompt_text: What do the illustrative cases show about the practical working of the Act?
self_check.expected_takeaway: That convictions are possible but penalising money laundering in practice is difficult and slow.
